lesson.title: Mental Shortcuts About Groups of People
lesson.summary: A stereotype is a generalized belief about the traits, behaviors, or characteristics of members of a group, a kind of cognitive shortcut that is efficient but that flattens the real variation that exists within any group of people.
lesson.body:
A schema, in general, is a mental structure that organizes what we know about a category, letting us process new information quickly by fitting it into an existing framework rather than reasoning from scratch every time. A stereotype is essentially a schema applied to a social group. It tells us, in advance and without new evidence, what a "typical" member of that group is supposedly like. Like other schemas, this can be cognitively efficient, letting us make fast predictions in a complex social world, but that efficiency comes at a real cost, since it papers over the enormous variation that exists among actual individuals within any group.

Social comparison helps explain how stereotypes take shape and persist. People naturally sort the social world into groups they belong to, in groups, and groups they do not belong to, out groups, and this basic sorting tendency shows up even in minimal, seemingly trivial group divisions studied by social psychologists. Once that sorting happens, comparisons between us and them become a major channel through which stereotypes form and get reinforced, often exaggerating differences between groups while minimizing the very real differences among individuals within each group.

It matters to be precise about what a stereotype actually is, because the terms stereotype, prejudice, and discrimination get conflated constantly in everyday speech. A stereotype is a belief, a cognitive judgment about what a group is like, "engineers are socially awkward," "older adults are bad with technology." It is distinct from prejudice, which is a feeling or attitude toward a group, and from discrimination, which is actual unfair behavior directed at members of a group. You can hold a stereotype without feeling hostility toward the group in question, and you can hold a stereotype without treating any individual unfairly because of it, though in practice stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination often travel together and reinforce one another, which is why the next two chapters look at each of the other two pieces in turn.

Stereotypes are also unusually resistant to correction. Some contain a grain of statistical truth about group averages, but the deeper problem is that they get applied to individuals regardless of whether a given person actually matches the average, and people tend to notice and remember information that confirms an existing stereotype while discounting or explaining away information that contradicts it. Combined with the fact that many stereotypes are absorbed secondhand, through media portrayals or cultural narratives, rather than through direct, varied experience with real people from a given group, this helps explain why stereotypes can persist stubbornly even in the face of a great deal of disconfirming evidence.
